en: One may live a hundred years
with no sīla and no samādhi.
Better it is a single day of life
for one who has sīla and meditates.
He rejoices here, he rejoices hereafter,
one who does good rejoices in both places.
He rejoices and is happy,
recollecting his pure deeds.
He is delighted here, he is delighted hereafter,
one who does good is delighted in both places.
[When thinking] “I have done good,” he is delighted,
when gone to a good destination, he is delighted even more.
All tremble at violence;
all fear death.
Seeing oneself in others,
one would neither kill nor cause another to kill.
All tremble at violence;
life is dear to all.
Seeing oneself in others,
one would neither kill nor cause another to kill.
Happiness is virtue until life’s end,
happiness is confidence well established,
happiness is the acquisition of wisdom,
and happiness is the avoidance of wrongdoing.

pali: dhīro pūrati puññassa, thokaṃ thokam’pi ācinaṃ.
en: Do not underestimate the good, thinking: “This will not come
to me”. Drop by drop, the water pot becomes full.
So too, the wise person fills himself with good,
gathering it little by little.
The non-doing of all bad actions,
the performance of the wholesome,
and the purification of one’s mind —
this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
I undertake the training precept of abstention from
the killing of beings.
I undertake the training precept of abstention from
the taking of what is not given.
I undertake the training precept of abstention from
sexual misconduct.
I undertake the training precept of abstention from
false speech.
I undertake the training precept of abstention from alcohol
and [other] intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One,
the fully Enlightened One.
I go for refuge to the Buddha.
I go for refuge to the Dhamma.
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
By practicing in accordance with the Dhamma:
I venerate the Buddha;
I venerate the Dhamma;
I venerate the Saṅgha.
The Buddhas of the past,
The Buddhas of the future,
The Buddhas of the present —
I always pay respects.
The Dhammas of the past,
The Dhammas of the future,
The Dhammas of the present —
I always pay respects.
The Saṅghas of the past,
The Saṅghas of the future,
The Saṅghas of the present —
I always pay respects.

bhagavato.dpd: Sublime One; Blessed One; Fortunate One; Auspicious One; epithet of the Buddha

en: That Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened,
accomplished in true knowledge and conduct,
fortunate, knower of the world,
unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed,
teacher of devas and humans,
the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.
The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One,
directly visible, immediate,
inviting one to come and see, applicable,
to be personally experienced by the wise.
The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples
is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way,
practicing the right way, practicing the proper way;
that is, the four pairs of persons,
the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha
of the Blessed One’s disciples
is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality,
worthy of offerings, worthy of reverence,
the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
“When a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata,
on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by craving,
not obsessed by aversion, not obsessed by delusion;
on that occasion his mind is simply straight,
based on the Tathāgata.
A noble disciple whose mind is straight gains inspiration
in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma,
gains joy connected with the Dhamma.
When he is joyful, rapture arises.
For one with a rapturous mind,
the body becomes tranquil.
One tranquil in body feels pleasure.
For one feeling pleasure,
the mind becomes concentrated.
This is called a noble disciple who dwells in balance
amid an unbalanced population,
who dwells unafflicted amid an afflicted population.
As one who has entered the stream of the Dhamma,
he develops recollection of the Buddha.
Again, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects the
Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well expounded by the
Blessed One…’
… recollects the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the
Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way…’”
“In a forest, at the foot of a tree,
or in an empty hut, O bhikkhus,
you should recollect the Buddha —
no fear will then arise in you.
But if you cannot recall the Buddha,
best in the world, the bull of men,
then you should recall the Dhamma,
emancipating, well expounded.
But if you cannot recall the Dhamma,
emancipating, well expounded,
then you should recall the Saṅgha,
the unsurpassed field of merit.
For those who thus recall the Buddha,
the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, bhikkhus,
no fear or trepidation will arise,
nor will their hair stand on end.”

pali: katame pañca? assutaṃ suṇāti; sutaṃ pariyodāpeti;
ime kho, bhikkhave, pañca ānisaṃsā dhamma-ssavane”ti.
en: “Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits in listening to the
Dhamma. What five? One hears what one has not heard;
one clarifies what has been heard; one overcomes
perplexity; one straightens out one’s view;
one’s mind becomes bright, calm and confident.
These are the five benefits in listening to the Dhamma.”

pali: ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sakkesu viharati kapilavatthusmiṃ,
nigrodh’ārāme. atha kho mahānāmo sakko yena bhagavā
en: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among
the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha’s Park. Then
Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One,

pali: nisīdi. ekam antaṃ nisinno kho, mahānāmo sakko
en: paid homage to him, sat down to one side,
and said to him:
“Venerable sir, in what way is one a lay follower?”

pali: “yato kho, mahānāma, buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti,
dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti
en: “When, Mahānāma, one has gone for refuge to
the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha,
one is then a lay follower.”
“In what way, venerable sir, is a lay follower
accomplished in virtue?”

pali: “yato kho, mahānāma, upāsako pāṇ’ātipātā paṭivirato hoti,
ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako sīla-sampanno hotī”ti.
en: “When, Mahānāma, a lay follower abstains from the
destruction of life, from taking what is not given,
from sexual misconduct, from false speech,
and from wines, liquor, and intoxicants that are
a basis for negligence, the lay follower is
accomplished in virtue.”
“In what way, venerable sir, is a lay follower
accomplished in devotion?”
“Here, Mahānāma, a lay follower is devoted;
he has confidence in the enlightenment of the
Tathāgata thus:
‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened,
accomplished in true knowledge and conduct,
fortunate, knower of the world,

pali: ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako saddhā-sampanno hotī”ti.
en: unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed,
teacher of devas and humans,
the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.’
In that way a lay follower is accomplished in devotion.”
“In what way, venerable sir, is a lay follower
accomplished in generosity?”

pali: ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako cāga-sampanno hotī”ti.
en: “Here, Mahānāma, a lay follower dwells at home with
a mind devoid of the stain of stinginess,
freely generous, open-handed, delighting in
relinquishment, one devoted to charity,
delighting in giving and sharing. In that way a lay
follower is accomplished in generosity.”
“In what way, venerable sir, is a lay follower
accomplished in wisdom?”

pali: ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako paññā-sampanno hotī”ti.
en: “Here, Mahānāma, a lay follower is wise,
he possesses wisdom directed to arising and
passing away, which is noble and penetrative,
leading to the complete destruction of dukkha.
In that way a lay follower is accomplished in wisdom.”
“There are, bhikkhus, these five gifts, great gifts,
primal, of long standing, traditional, ancient,
unsullied and never before sullied,
which are not being sullied, and will not be sullied,
not rejected by wise ascetics and brahmins.

pali: katamāni pañca? idha, bhikkhave, ariya-sāvako pāṇ’ātipātaṃ
pahāya, pāṇ’ātipātā paṭivirato hoti. pāṇ’ātipātā paṭivirato,
abhayaṃ deti, averaṃ deti, abyābajjhaṃ deti.
en: What five? Here, a noble disciple, having abandoned
the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction
of life. By abstaining from the destruction of life,
the noble disciple gives to an immeasurable number
of beings freedom from fear, enmity, and affliction.

pali: aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ abhayaṃ datvā, averaṃ datvā,
idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ dānaṃ mahā-dānaṃ ... pe ...
en: Having given to an immeasurable number of beings
freedom from fear, enmity, and affliction,
he himself in turn enjoys immeasurable freedom
from fear, enmity, and affliction.
This is the first gift, a great gift ...

pali: puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariya-sāvako adinn’ādānaṃ pahāya
en: Again, a noble disciple, having abandoned the taking
of what is not given, abstains from taking what is not
given … abstains from sexual misconduct … abstains
from false speech … abstains from liquor, wine, and
intoxicants, the basis for negligence.
By abstaining from liquor, wine, and intoxicants,
the basis for negligence, the noble disciple gives
to an immeasurable number of beings freedom
from fear, enmity, and affliction.

pali: aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ abhayaṃ datvā, averaṃ datvā,
abyābajjhassa bhāgī hoti. idaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcamaṃ dānaṃ,
asaṃkiṇṇaṃ, asaṃkiṇṇapubbaṃ, na saṃkiyati na saṃkiyissati,
en: He himself in turn enjoys immeasurable freedom
from fear, enmity, and affliction. This is the fifth gift,
a great gift, primal, of long standing, traditional,
ancient, unadulterated and never before adulterated,
which is not being adulterated and will not be
adulterated, not rejected by wise ascetics and
brahmins.”
“Bhikkhus, abandon the unwholesome!
It is possible to abandon the unwholesome.

pali: no ce’daṃ, bhikkhave, sakkā abhavissa akusalaṃ pajahituṃ,
en: If it were not possible to abandon the unwholesome,
I would not say:
‘Bhikkhus, abandon the unwholesome!’

pali: yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, sakkā akusalaṃ pajahituṃ,
en: But because it is possible to abandon the
unwholesome, I say:
‘Bhikkhus, abandon the unwholesome!’

pali: akusalañ ca h’idaṃ, bhikkhave, pahīnaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya
en: If this abandoning of the unwholesome led to harm
and dukkha, I would not tell you to abandon it.

pali: yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, akusalaṃ pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya
en: But because the abandoning of the unwholesome
leads to welfare and happiness,
I say: ‘Bhikkhus, abandon the unwholesome!’

pali: no ce’daṃ, bhikkhave, sakkā abhavissa kusalaṃ bhāvetuṃ,
yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, sakkā kusalaṃ bhāvetuṃ,
en: Bhikkhus, develop the wholesome!
It is possible to develop the wholesome.
If it were not possible to develop the wholesome,
I would not say: ‘Bhikkhus, develop the wholesome!’
But because it is possible to develop the wholesome,
I say: ‘Bhikkhus, develop the wholesome!’

pali: kusalañ ca h’idaṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvitaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya
‘kusalaṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvethā’ti. yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave,
en: If this developing of the wholesome led to harm and
dukkha, I would not tell you to develop it.
But because the developing of the wholesome leads
to welfare and happiness,
I say: ‘Bhikkhus, develop the wholesome!’”

pali: evaṃ me sutaṃ. ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ
en: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was
dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

pali: atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā ten’upasaṅkami;
en: Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One,
paid homage to him, sat down to one side,

pali: ekam antaṃ nisinno kho, āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ
en: and said to him:
(1) “Bhante, what is the purpose and benefit of
wholesome virtuous behavior?”
(2) “Ānanda, the purpose and benefit of wholesome
virtuous behavior is non-regret.”
(3) “And what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of
non-regret?”
“The purpose and benefit of non-regret is joy.”
(4) “And what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of joy?”
“The purpose and benefit of joy is rapture.”
(5) “And what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of
rapture?”
“The purpose and benefit of rapture is tranquility.”
(6) “And what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of
tranquility?”
“The purpose and benefit of tranquility is pleasure.”
(7) “And what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of
pleasure?”
“The purpose and benefit of pleasure is concentration.”
(8) “And what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of
concentration?”
“The purpose and benefit of concentration is the
knowledge and vision of things as they really are.”
(9) “And what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of the
knowledge and vision of things as they really are?”
“The purpose and benefit of the knowledge and vision of
things as they really are is disenchantment.”
(10) And what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of
disenchantment?”
“The purpose and benefit of disenchantment is
dispassion.”
(11) “And what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of
dispassion?”
“The purpose and benefit of dispassion is the knowledge
and vision of liberation.”

pali: iti kho, ānanda, kusalāni sīlāni avippaṭisār’atthāni
en: “Thus, Ānanda, (1)–(2) the purpose and benefit of
wholesome virtuous behavior is non-regret;
(3) the purpose and benefit of non-regret is joy;
(4) the purpose and benefit of joy is rapture;
(5) the purpose and benefit of rapture is tranquility;
(6) the purpose and benefit of tranquility is pleasure;
(7) the purpose and benefit of pleasure is concentration;
(8) the purpose and benefit of concentration is the
knowledge and vision of things as they really are;
(9) the purpose and benefit of the knowledge and vision
of things as they really are is disenchantment; (10) the
purpose and benefit of disenchantment is dispassion;

pali: iti kho, ānanda, kusalāni sīlāni anupubbena aggāya
en: and (11) the purpose and benefit of dispassion is the
knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thus, Ānanda, wholesome virtuous behavior progressively
leads to the foremost.”

pali: kathañ ca, bhikkhave, sammā-diṭṭhi pubbaṅgamā hoti?
en: “Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first.
And how does right view come first?
One understands wrong action as wrong action and
right action as right action:
this is one’s right view. […]

pali: sā’ssa hoti sammā-sati. itiyime tayo dhammā
en: One makes an effort to abandon wrong action and to
enter upon right action: this is one’s right effort.
Aware, one abandons wrong action,
aware, one enters upon and abides in right action:
this is one’s right awareness.
Thus these three things run and circle around right
action, that is, right view, right effort, and right
awareness. …”
“Not associating with fools,
associating with the wise,
and venerating those worthy of veneration:
this is the highest blessing.
Residing in a suitable place,
merit done in the past,
and directing oneself rightly:
this is the highest blessing.
Much learning, a craft,
well-trained discipline,
and well-spoken speech:
this is the highest blessing.
Serving one’s mother and father,
supporting one’s wife and children,
and an honest occupation:
this is the highest blessing.
Giving and righteous conduct,
assistance to relatives,
blameless deeds:
this is the highest blessing.
Desisting and abstaining from bad actions,
refraining from intoxicating drink,
diligence in good qualities:
this is the highest blessing.
Reverence and humility,
contentment and gratitude,
timely listening to the Dhamma:
this is the highest blessing.
Patience, being amenable to advice,
the seeing of ascetics,
timely discussion on the Dhamma:
this is the highest blessing.
Ardent practice and the spiritual life,
seeing of the noble truths,
and realization of nibbāna:
this is the highest blessing.
One whose mind does not shake
when touched by worldly conditions,
sorrowless, stainless, secure:
this is the highest blessing.
Those who have done these things
are victorious everywhere;
everywhere they go safely:
theirs is that highest blessing.”
One should guard against angry speech,
let one be restrained in speech.
Abandoning verbal misconduct,
one should practice good conduct in speech.
One is not wise because one speaks much.
One who is peaceful,
kind and fearless
is called wise.
Just as a lovely flower, beautiful but without fragrance,
so too, well-spoken words bring no good results
for one who doesn’t act accordingly.
Just as a lovely flower, beautiful and fragrant,
so too, well-spoken words have good results
for one who acts accordingly.
Better than a thousand meaningless words,
is a single meaningful word,
upon hearing it,
one finds peace.

tatra.dpd: there; in that place; in that case

pali: “… evameva kho, rāja-kumāra, yaṃ tathāgato vācaṃ
en: “… So too, prince, such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial,
and which is also unwelcome and disagreeable to others:
such speech the Tathāgata does not utter.

pali: yam’pi tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ, tacchaṃ,
anattha-saṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā,
en: Such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be true and correct but unbeneficial,
and which is also unwelcome and disagreeable to others:
such speech the Tathāgata does not utter.

pali: yañ ca kho tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ, tacchaṃ,
attha-saṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā,
tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāya.
en: Such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be true, correct, and beneficial,
but which is unwelcome and disagreeable to others:
the Tathāgata knows the time to use such speech.

pali: yaṃ tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti abhūtaṃ, atacchaṃ,
anattha-saṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā,
en: Such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial,
but which is welcome and agreeable to others:
such speech the Tathāgata does not utter.

pali: yam’pi tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ, tacchaṃ,
anattha-saṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā,
en: Such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be true and correct but unbeneficial,
and which is welcome and agreeable to others:
such speech the Tathāgata does not utter.

pali: yañ ca tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ, tacchaṃ,
attha-saṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā,
tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāya.
en: Such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be true, correct, and beneficial,
and which is welcome and agreeable to others:
the Tathāgata knows the time to use such speech.
Why is that?
Because the Tathāgata has compassion for beings.” […]
“… Bhikkhus, it is not suitable for you, respectable
people who have gone forth from the household life
into homelessness out of faith, to engage in various
kinds of pointless talk, that is: talk about kings,
thieves… wars; talk about food, drink, clothes… talk
about garlands and scents; talk about relatives,
vehicles, villages, towns… miscellaneous talk; tales
of land and sea; talk about becoming this or that.
There are, bhikkhus, these ten topics for discussion.
What ten? Talk on fewness of desires, contentment,
solitude, non-entanglement, arousing energy,
virtuous behavior, concentration, wisdom,
liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation.
These are the ten topics for discussion.”

no.note: Here no is the pronoun “our”, not the word for “not”.

en: “Bhikkhus, there are these five courses of speech
that others may use when they address you:
their speech may be timely or untimely,
true or untrue,
gentle or harsh,
connected with good or with harm,
spoken with a mind of mettā or with inner hate. […]

pali: hit’ānukampī ca viharissāma metta-cittā, na dos’antarā.
en: Herein, bhikkhus, you should train thus:
‘Our minds will remain unaffected, and we shall utter
no harmful words; compassionate for their welfare,
we shall dwell with a mind of mettā, without inner hate.

pali: tañ ca puggalaṃ mettā-sahagatena cetasā pharitvā
en: We shall dwell pervading that person with a mind
suffused with mettā, and starting with him,
we shall dwell pervading the all-encompassing world
with a mind suffused with mettā, abundant, exalted,
boundless, without hostility and without ill-will.’
That is how you should train, bhikkhus.

pali: tatr’āpi yo mano padūseyya, na me so tena sāsana-karo.
en: Bhikkhus, even if mean bandits were to sever you limb
by limb with a two-handled saw, one who gave rise to
a mind of hate towards them would not be acting
according to my teaching.

pali: ‘na c’eva no cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ bhavissati … pe …’
en: Herein, bhikkhus, you should train thus:
‘Our minds will remain unaffected …’
That is how you should train, bhikkhus.”

suttas.title: hadayaṅgamā vācā
suttas.en: Words That Go to the Heart

en: “… Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false
speech; he speaks truth, adheres to truth;
he is trustworthy and reliable, no deceiver of the world.
This, too, is there in his sīla.

pali: pisuṇaṃ vācaṃ pahāya, pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti;
ito sutvā, na amutra akkhātā, imesaṃ bhedāya;
amutra vā sutvā, na imesaṃ akkhātā, amūsaṃ bhedāya.
en: Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from
divisive speech; if he hears something here, he does not
repeat it elsewhere in order to divide [those people] from
these; if he hears something elsewhere, he does not repeat
it to these people here, in order to divide them from those;

pali: iti bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātā, sahitānaṃ vā anuppadātā,
en: thus he is one who reunites those who are divided,
a promoter of unity, who enjoys harmony,
rejoices in harmony, delights in harmony,
a speaker of words that promote harmony.
This, too, is there in his sīla.

pali: pharusaṃ vācaṃ pahāya, pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato
hoti; yā sā vācā nelā, kaṇṇa-sukhā,
en: Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh
speech; he speaks words that are gentle,
pleasing to the ear, lovable, words that go to the heart,
courteous words that are cherished by many people
and agreeable to many people.
This, too, is there in his sīla.

pali: vinaya-vādī, nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti, kālena,
en: Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle
chatter; he speaks at a proper time, speaks what is truthful,
speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma,
speaks on the discipline; at the proper time he speaks
such words as are worth treasuring, reasonable,
to the point, and beneficial.
This, too, is there in his sīla.”
Regard the one who sees your faults
as a guide to hidden treasure;
associate with such a wise one
who points out your mistakes.
It is better, not worse,
to associate with such a wise person.

assa.dpd: could be; may be; might be; should be
assa.note: evam assa: “it may be thus”, i.e. if this occurs to you. Elsewhere assa is the pronoun “his”.

en: “While you are training in harmony,
with mutual appreciation, without disputing,
some bhikkhu might commit an offence or a transgression.
Now, bhikkhus, you should not hurry to criticize him;
rather, the person should be examined thus: (1)
‘I shall not be troubled
and the other person will not be hurt;
for the other person is not angry and resentful,
he is not firmly attached to his view
and he relinquishes easily,

pali: sakkomi c’āhaṃ etaṃ puggalaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā
sace, bhikkhave, evam assa, kallaṃ vacanāya.
en: and I can make that person emerge from the
unwholesome and establish him in the wholesome.’
If such occurs to you, bhikkhus, it is proper to speak.

pali: sakkomi c’āhaṃ etaṃ puggalaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā
en: Then it may occur to you, bhikkhus: (2)
‘I shall not be troubled,
but the other person will be hurt;
for the other person is angry and resentful.
However, he is not firmly attached to his view
and he relinquishes easily,
and I can make that person emerge from the
unwholesome and establish him in the wholesome.

pali: atha kho etadeva bahutaraṃ — so’haṃ sakkomi etaṃ
sace, bhikkhave, evam assa, kallaṃ vacanāya.
en: It is a minor matter that the other person will be hurt,
but it is a much greater thing that I can make that
person emerge from the unwholesome and establish
him in the wholesome.’
If such occurs to you, bhikkhus, it is proper to speak.

pali: sakkomi c’āhaṃ etaṃ puggalaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā
en: Then it may occur to you, bhikkhus: (3)
‘I shall be troubled,
but the other person will not be hurt;
for the other person is not angry and resentful,
though he is firmly attached to his view
and he relinquishes with difficulty;
yet I can make that person emerge from the unwholesome
and establish him in the wholesome.

pali: mayhaṃ vihesā. atha kho etadeva bahutaraṃ —
so’haṃ sakkomi etaṃ puggalaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā
sace, bhikkhave, evam assa, kallaṃ vacanāya.
en: It is a minor matter that I shall be troubled,
but it is a much greater thing that I can make that
person emerge from the unwholesome
and establish him in the wholesome.’
If such occurs to you, bhikkhus, it is proper to speak.

pali: sakkomi c’āhaṃ etaṃ puggalaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā
en: Then it may occur to you, bhikkhus: (4)
‘I shall be troubled and the other person will be hurt;
for the other person is angry and resentful,
and he is firmly attached to his view
and he relinquishes with difficulty;
yet I can make that person emerge from the unwholesome
and establish him in the wholesome.

pali: atha kho etadeva bahutaraṃ — so’haṃ sakkomi etaṃ
sace, bhikkhave, evam assa, kallaṃ vacanāya.
en: It is a minor matter that I shall be troubled and the other
person hurt, but it is a much greater thing that I can
make that person emerge from the unwholesome
and establish him in the wholesome.’
If such occurs to you, bhikkhus, it is proper to speak.

pali: daḷha-diṭṭhī duppaṭinissaggī, na c’āhaṃ sakkomi etaṃ
en: Then it may occur to you, bhikkhus: (5)
‘I shall be troubled and the other person will be hurt;
for the other person is angry and resentful,
and he is firmly attached to his view
and he relinquishes with difficulty;
and I cannot make that person emerge from the
unwholesome and establish him in the wholesome.’
One should not underrate equanimity towards
such a person.”

pali: “pañca kho ime, bhāradvāja, dhammā diṭṭh’eva dhamme
pañca dhammā diṭṭh’eva dhamme dvedhā vipākā.
en: “There are five things, Bhāradvāja, that may turn out in
two different ways here and now. What five?
Faith, liking, oral tradition, logical reasoning,
and reflective acceptance of a view. These five things may
turn out in two different ways here and now.

pali: tañ ca hoti rittaṃ, tucchaṃ, musā;
tañ ca hoti bhūtaṃ, tacchaṃ, anaññathā.
en: Now something may be fully accepted out of faith,
yet it may be empty, hollow, and false;
but something else may not be fully accepted out of faith,
yet it may be factual, true, and unmistaken.

pali: api ca, bhāradvāja, surucitaṃyeva hoti … pe …
… pe … sunijjhāyitaṃyeva hoti, tañ ca hoti rittaṃ,
tucchaṃ, musā; no ce’pi sunijjhāyitaṃ hoti,
tañ ca hoti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ anaññathā.
en: Again, something may be liked very much …
well transmitted … well cogitated …
well reflected upon, yet it may be empty, hollow,
and false; but something else may not be well reflected
upon, yet it may be factual, true, and unmistaken.
[Under these conditions] it is not proper for a wise man
who protects truth to come to the definite conclusion:
‘Only this is true, anything else is wrong.’”
“But, Master Gotama, in what way is there the protection
of truth? How does one protect truth?
We ask Master Gotama about the protection of truth.”

pali: ‘evaṃ me saddhā’ti — iti vadaṃ saccam anurakkhati,
na tveva tāva ek’aṃsena niṭṭhaṃ gacchati:
en: “If a person has faith, Bhāradvāja, he protects truth when
he says: ‘My faith is thus’;
but he does not yet come to the definite conclusion:
‘Only this is true, anything else is wrong.’
In this way, Bhāradvāja, there is the protection of truth;
in this way he protects truth;
in this way we describe the protection of truth;
but as yet there is no awakening to truth.

pali: ruci ce’pi, bhāradvāja, purisassa hoti … pe …
anussavo ce’pi, bhāradvāja, purisassa hoti … pe …
ākāra-parivitakko ce’pi, bhāradvāja, purisassa hoti … pe …
na tveva tāva ek’aṃsena niṭṭhaṃ gacchati:
en: If a person has a liking for something … if he receives an
oral tradition … if he uses logical reasoning …
if he gains a reflective acceptance of a view,
he protects truth when he says:
‘My reflective acceptance of a view is thus’;
but he does not yet come to the definite conclusion:
‘Only this is true, anything else is wrong.’
In this way too, Bhāradvāja, there is the protection of
truth; in this way he protects truth;
in this way we describe the protection of truth. …”

pali: kathañ ca, bhikkhave, sammā-diṭṭhi pubbaṅgamā hoti?
en: “Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first.
And how does right view come first?
One understands wrong speech as wrong speech and
right speech as right speech:
this is one’s right view. […]

pali: upasampadāya; sv’āssa hoti sammā-vāyāmo. so sato
viharati; sā’ssa hoti sammā-sati. itiyime tayo dhammā
en: One makes an effort to abandon wrong speech and
to enter upon right speech: this is one’s right effort.
Aware, one abandons wrong speech,
aware, one enters upon and abides in right speech:
this is one’s right awareness. Thus these three things
run and circle around right speech, that is, right view,
right effort, and right awareness. …”
